title: The AI trade selloff is taking more than tech stocks down with it
excerpt: Copper is trading increasingly like an AI stock, with investors retreating from bullish bets even as physical supplies remain tight in China.
content_html:
By Huileng Tan

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-18T05:25:04.834Z

The AI stock selloff is spilling into commodity markets, putting pressure on copper and other metals that had benefited from expectations of a massive infrastructure boom.

Copper, used in data-center power systems and electrical grids, has fallen 11% from its September record. Tin, essential for soldering electronic components, and aluminum have also come under pressure amid a broader retreat in industrial metals.

The reversal follows a blockbuster 2025 for metals. Benchmark copper futures on the London Metal Exchange ended the year 35% higher, buoyed by supply constraints, tariff uncertainty, and expectations of growing demand from electrification and AI infrastructure.

On Tuesday, LME copper fell to $13,144 a metric ton, its lowest since early July, as weakness in technology stocks weighed on sentiment.

LME aluminum has fallen to its lowest level in about a year, while tin touched its lowest since March.

A stronger dollar, expectations of higher US interest rates, and sluggish Chinese economic data have also added to pressure on industrial metals.

Copper is trading like an AI stock

Copper prices have tracked a basket of AI data-center stocks since late 2025, suggesting that sentiment toward the technology boom is influencing the metal's price, Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note last week.

The red metal's recent decline has been "largely driven by the volatility in AI-related equities," they added.

That retreat is also evident in the futures market, where investors have sharply reduced their bullish bets on copper.

Net bullish positions in copper futures on the London Metal Exchange and Comex fell from about 21% of outstanding contracts at the end of September to just 9% in early November, according to Goldman.

The sharp reduction suggests that some of copper's recent weakness reflects investors unwinding bets on higher prices, rather than a sudden deterioration in demand for the metal.

That's as physical supplies remain tight in parts of the market, particularly China.

"We see the recent correction as positioning-driven rather than reflecting loosening fundamentals," Goldman said.

Copper import premiums in China have jumped to a record high, while copper inventories on the Shanghai Futures Exchange have fallen to their lowest since December 2023.

Part of the supply squeeze reflects where the world's copper is being stored. Much of the metal held in exchange warehouses has accumulated in the US ahead of potential tariffs, leaving supplies less readily available elsewhere.

Goldman is maintaining its forecast for copper to reach $15,400 a ton in 2027.
